title: The second jhana
hookLine: a lake fed by a spring from within (MN 39)

cards: Some lakes are filled by rivers: water pours down from the hills, and if the rivers dry up, the lake shrinks. Some are topped up by rain. And some are filled from beneath.
A cold spring wells up from the lakebed, and the lake stays full even in a dry season. You can't see where the water is coming from. It just keeps arriving.

teach.b: In MN 39 the Buddha describes the next stage.

With the stilling of directed and sustained thought, a person enters the second jhana: inner confidence, the mind become one, without directed or sustained thought, with joy and pleasure born of concentration.
Then his picture: a lake whose waters well up from below. No stream flows in from the east, the west, the north or the south.
The sky doesn't fill it with rain from time to time. But a cool spring wells up within it and soaks the whole lake, so that no part is left untouched. Set it beside yesterday's picture.
In the first jhana, water was added by a hand, sprinkled and kneaded into the powder, and the joy was born of seclusion, of stepping away. Here the hand is gone.
Thinking has gone quiet, and the joy is born of concentration itself; it rises from inside. Two Pali words carry this.
Sampasadana: inner clearness, or inner confidence; one way to picture it is muddy water settling until you can see the bottom. And ekodibhava: the mind becoming single, unified.
The calm doesn't depend on anything outside: no good news, no compliment, no perfect weather.
In SN 21.1, Moggallana tells how he came to see that the second jhana is what's called noble silence.
Not the silence of a closed mouth, but of a mind that has stopped talking to itself.

how: Meditators who train in the jhanas usually do so under a teacher's guidance, often on retreat; many Buddhists also use the phrase 'noble silence' for periods of silence kept at retreats.

o: inner clearness, like muddy water settling
a gift given to a teacher in gratitude
the joy of hearing good news from outside

p: a lake fed by a spring
a name for the second jhana

s: in the second jhana, directed and sustained thought go still
that stilling is what marks the move from the first.
the lake in the simile is kept full by rain
no stream, no rain: a cool spring wells up from within.
by the second jhana, the joy is gone
joy and pleasure remain, now born of concentration.

games.q: a lake has no streams flowing in and gets no rain. how does it stay full, in the Buddha's simile?
o: it doesn't; it slowly dries up
a cool spring wells up from within it
games.why: the spring rises from inside and soaks the whole lake. the calm of the second jhana needs nothing poured in from outside.

practice: Let the breath settle, and when a thought comes, let it pass without picking it up.

Between thoughts there may be small gaps, a breath or two with nothing to do; rest in one and notice whether anything wells up on its own, quiet, coolness, a little gladness, and if nothing does, the gap itself is enough.

wordCard.voice: Sampasadana, inner clearness. Thinking grows still, and joy wells up from within, like a lake fed by its own spring.

orig.note: Pali sampasādana: inner clearness or confidence, like water settling clear; a quality of the second jhāna.

carryVoice: Your line: the inner spring. A calm that depends on nothing outside, welling up from within. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 39, Maha-Assapura Sutta (the spring-fed lake)
